Ergo opus est seutica [?]: justis hanc plectite flagris O Socii! Injectis frenate sophisma lupatis! Eximius Doctor præit Hottingerus, & adstat Præstes, qui tanti mensuram nominis implet. Hinc exurget honos, hinc tempora laurea cinget. Christe, Dei Fili, tu nostram, dirige cymbam, Clementer dextram mento suppone natanti! Da te Navarchâ felicia littora tangat Nostra ratis: Laudémque tuam cantabimus usque!
units.tr: Foul superstition, daughter of murky night, after lifting her deadly head out of the Stygian waves, has overturned everything, casting Jove behind her back under the cloak of painted wisdom; and the doctrines of a frenzied mind have begun to be knotted together at their very borders. Therefore there is need of the scourge: strike this sophistry with just lashes, O comrades! Curb it with bridles put on it! The distinguished Teacher Hottinger goes before us, and the Praeses stands beside him, who fills the measure of so great a name. From this will rise honour; from this a laurel will crown our brows. Christ, Son of God, direct our bark; mercifully place your right hand beneath the chin of us who swim! Grant that our raft, with you as pilot, may reach happy shores, and we shall sing your praise forever!

units.tr: The doctrine of the sophistical or deceptive syllogism [σοφιστικῶν ἢ ἀπατηλικῶν]: those who discard logic do not see the hiding-places (a) and snares (b) that they prepare for their opponents.

units.la: [a] Quæ mens est Rami & Ramæorum ; quibus oppone Kecker, præcog. Log. tract. III. p. 219. Burgersd. Inst. Log. l. II. c. 25. Dicter. lib II. p. 315. & alios.
units.tr: [a] This is the view of Ramus and the Ramists. Set against them Keckermann, Praecognita Logicae, tract. III, p. 219; Burgersdijk, Institutiones Logicae, l. II, c. 25; Dicterich, lib. II, p. 315; and others.

units.la: [b] Neque enim impostores his facilè valedicent artibus, etsi nullis nostri contra eas muniantur ἀμυνταρίοις. Videmus, studio & arte fucata ejusmodi, sophismata; tincta tela, elisa etiã, ab adversariis repeti; quid fiat, si tyrones nostri hæc arma tractare ne quidem didicerint? Audaciores certò reddent πλάνες istos, & ad nocendum ferociores. Idem ergo est officium boni Logici, quod esse scribit Epiphanius initio Panar. boni Medici & Theologi. Nicander, inquit, scriptor, bestiarum & reptilium naturas cognitas fecit. Alii verò scriptores de radicibus & herbis prodiderunt velut Dioscorides materiarius, Pamphilus, ac Mithridates Rex, Callisthenes & Philo, Iolaus item Bithynus, & Heraclides Tarentinus, Cratevas herbarius, Andreas, Basius Tylius, Niceratus, Petronius, Niger, Diodotus & alii quidam. Eodem modo etiam nos Sectarum radices & opiniones revelare conantes, non in detrimentum legentium, sed velut relati scriptores studio habuerunt, non ut malum indicarent, sed ad timorem & cautionem humanæ naturæ, ut mala & perniciosa cognoscerent homines, seq. præmunirent, & per potentiam DEI effugerent, per animadversionem & repudiationem. At si qui in talia jam incidissent, & ab ejusmodi insidias pertulissent, aut per insufflationem, aut per morsum, aut aspectum: iidem de his solliciti, auxiliares radices ac herbas praescripserunt, ad praedictorum reptilium improbitates irritas faciendas. Sic etiam nobis studium est, per relatorum, & vestram, dilectissimi fratres, exhortationem, ut malorum reptilium ac bestiarum tum formas tristes, tum morsus lethales revelemus. Ad oppositionem vero horum quacunque possumus in compendio dicere, unum atque alterum verbum ad repellendum ipsorum venenum & servandum eum, qui Dominum sequi velit, sive ex sua sententia, sive invitus in eadem reptilia haeresion ac sectarum dogmata illapsum instar antidotorum apponemus. Hac Methodo, hoc scopo & usu Logicus doctrinam de Fallaciis proponit & propinat.
units.tr: [b] Indeed, deceivers will not readily give up these arts, even though none of ours is armed against them with antidotes [ἀμυντηρίοις]. We see that sophisms of this kind, dyed and polished by study and craft, are taken up again by opponents, their weapons blunted as well as sharpened. What would happen if our novices had not even learned to handle these weapons? They would surely make those deceivers [πλάνης] bolder and fiercer in doing harm. The office of a good logician is therefore the same as, according to Epiphanius at the beginning of the Panarion, that of a good physician and theologian. Nicander, he says, the writer, made known the natures of beasts and reptiles. Other writers, however, have handed down accounts of roots and herbs, such as Dioscorides the herbalist, Pamphilus, and King Mithridates, Callisthenes and Philo, likewise Iolaus of Bithynia, and Heraclides of Tarentum, Crateuas the herbalist, Andreas, Basius Tylius, Niceratus, Petronius, Niger, Diodotus and certain others. In the same way we too, trying to reveal the roots and opinions of the sects, have not done so to the harm of the readers, but, like those writers mentioned, have pursued this study not to recommend the evil, but for the fear and caution of human nature, so that people might know evil and pernicious things, forearm themselves, and by the power of God escape them, through attention and rejection. But if any had already fallen into such things and suffered from such snares, either by breath, or by bite, or by sight, those who cared for them prescribed helpful roots and herbs to render void the malice of the aforesaid reptiles. So too it is our aim, through the instruction of those who have been told, and through your exhortation, dearest brothers, to reveal both the grim shapes and the deadly bites of the evil reptiles and beasts. As for opposing them, we can say briefly in as many words as we can, one or another word to repel their poison and to preserve whoever wishes to follow the Lord, and we will set down, like antidotes, whether in our own judgment or against our will, the dogmas of heresies and sects that have slipped in among those same reptiles. By this method, with this aim and this use, the logician sets forth and serves up the doctrine of fallacies.

We should like to bring the Papacy onto the stage as a specimen, for if you remove its fallacies, little will remain to sustain it. IV. But since others have performed this task with praise and have reaped this field with their sickle, we will run over the whole field of fallacies, content with a gleaning, if human industry has left anything.

units.la: V. Fallaciae autem committuntur vel in Forma, vel in Materia. Illæ, cum Leges Syllogisticæ violantur; hæ vel in verbis apparent, vel in rebus. Unde Fallacia Materiae iterum est vel in dictione, vel exextra dictionem. Fallaciæ in dictione numerantur Sex 1. Homonymiæ. 2. Amphiboliæ. 3 Compositionis. 4. Divisionis. 5. Accentus. 6. Figuræ Dictionis. Fallaciæ extra dictionem sunt septem. 1. Fallacia Accidentis. 2. A dicto secundùm quid ad dictum simpliciter. 3. Ignoratio Elenchi. 4. Petitio principii. 5. Consequentiæ. 6. A non causa ut causa. 7. A pluribus interrogationibus.
units.tr: V. Fallacies are committed either in form or in matter. The former occur when the rules of syllogism are violated; the latter appear either in words or in things. Hence a fallacy of matter is again either within the diction or outside the diction. There are six fallacies within the diction: (1) equivocation; (2) amphiboly; (3) composition; (4) division; (5) accent; (6) figure of speech. There are seven fallacies outside the diction: (1) fallacy of accident; (2) from what is said in a certain respect to what is said absolutely; (3) ignorance of refutation; (4) begging the question; (5) consequent; (6) non-cause as cause; (7) from many questions.

units.la: VI. Fallacia Homonymiæ ex unius tantùm vocis ambiguitate oritur.
units.tr: VI. The fallacy of equivocation arises from the ambiguity of a single word alone.

units.la: Ex hac enim quatuor statim emergunt termini, quos Syllogistica forma non fert. Atque huc pertinent I. Omnes voces ambiguæ, sive ἀπὸ τύχης, sive ἐκ προσωπέσεως tales, Metaphoricæ cumprimis, quæ vel subjectum reddunt ambiguum, vel PræPredicatum, vel Medium. Unde tripliciter Homonymia contingere potest. II. Quæstiones seu interrogationes captiosæ; Cessâsti furari, annon? Sive affirmes, sive neges, in luto hæres; nisi distinctione emerseris. Hac ambiguitate ludunt Pontificii A contra fidem justificantem: Charitas est major fide. E. Fides magis justificat. Fidei enim vox 1.Cor.13.v.2. non fiduciam significat, sed fidem miraculorum. Latet & fallacia à dicto secundùm quid ad dictum simpliciter, item à non causa ut causa. Vide Calvin. Instit. 1.3.c 18.S.8. B. pro merito operum, maximè dilectionis, Col.3.v.14. ἡ ἀγάπη ἐστὶ σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος: Homonymia est in Prædicato perfectionis, quæ ad Ecclesiæ εὐρυθμίαν pertinet & complementum, non verò ad causas nostræ justificationis. Vide Cal.l.c. C. Pro cæco obsequio Ecclesiæ debito. Voci Ecclesiæ parendum est. Ceremoniæ, ritus, &c. sunt vox Ecclesiæ. Vox enim ὁμωνύμως sumitur. Si ἐγγεγραμμένον est, ex Mosis Cathedra pronunciata concedimus Matth.23.2. Sed si ἀγςαφῷ non modò, sed & ἀνπγςαφῷ, si fermentum, negamus; Matth.16.5.&12.
units.tr: For from this four terms at once emerge, which the syllogistic form does not admit. To this belong: I. all ambiguous words, whether ambiguous by chance [ἀπὸ τύχης] or by figure of speech [ἐκ προσωπέσεως], metaphorical ones especially, which make either the subject, or the predicate, or the middle term ambiguous. Hence equivocation can arise in three ways. II. Captious questions or interrogations: "Have you stopped stealing, or not?" Whether you affirm or deny, you stick in the mud unless you get out by a distinction. The Papists play on this ambiguity against justifying faith: "Charity is greater than faith. Therefore faith justifies more. Faith" (for the word faith in 1 Cor. 13:2 signifies not trust but the faith of miracles). The fallacy from what is said in a certain respect to what is said absolutely lies hidden here too, and also that from non-cause as cause. See Calvin, Institutes 3.18.8, B. Regarding the merit of works, especially of love, Col. 3:14: "love is the bond of perfection" [ἡ ἀγάπη ἐστὶ σύνδεσμος τῆς τελειότητος]: equivocation is in the predicate "perfection," which pertains to the good order and completion of the Church, and not to the causes of our justification. See Calvin, loc. cit., C. Regarding the blind obedience owed to the Church: one must obey the voice of the Church. Ceremonies, rites, etc. are the voice of the Church, for voice is taken equivocally. If it is written, we concede that it is pronounced from Moses' seat, Matt. 23:2. But if it is unwritten, not only unwritten but even contrary to what is written, such as leaven [ἀγράφῳ], we deny it: Matt. 16:5, 12.

units.la: VII. Fallacia Amphibolia, cùm dubia plurium vo- cùm sententia ambiguos efficit terminos.
units.tr: VII. The fallacy of amphiboly, when the doubtful sense of several words makes the terms ambiguous.

units.la: Vocatur aliàs ambiguitas Syntaxeos, quæ committitur 1. cùm ipsa orationis syntaxis est ambigua. 2. quando phrasis aut sermonis genus parit sententiæ incertitudinem. Prioris generis sallaciam struunt Pontificii, liberi arbitrii patroni, ex illo Gen.4. v.7. ubi Deus ad Cainum: Appetitus ejus super te; & imperabis ei. E sibi, suæque voluntati imperat homo. Fallacia est Amphibolia, ex ambiguitate constructionis nata. Affixum enim vau non ad peccatum, sed ad Abelem referri debet. Eadem etiam chorda oberrant Judæi. Vide Anal p.92. Calvin. Instit. l.2.c.5.S.16. Posterioris classis amplam præbet segetem ignorantia Idiotismorum Græcorum & Hebraicorum, quæ multa errorum portenta in Ecclesiam invexit. Sit exemplo trita illa captio, Gen.48.16. Voluit Jacob nomen suum post mortem invocari super liberis suis. E mortui possunt invocari. Ineptus est paralogismus, quem linguæ Hebrææ peperit ignorantia, cujus ipsosmet pudere cœpit emunctiorum narium Doctores Pontificios. Vide. Anal.p.213.
units.tr: It is also called ambiguity of syntax, and it is committed (1) when the syntax of the sentence itself is ambiguous, and (2) when a phrase or a kind of speech produces uncertainty of meaning. The Papists and the defenders of free will build a fallacy of the first kind on Gen. 4. v. 7, where God says to Cain: Its desire is toward you, and you shall rule over it. From this they conclude that man rules over himself and his own will. It is a fallacy of amphiboly, arising from the ambiguity of the construction, for the suffix vau must be referred not to sin but to Abel. The Jews too go astray on this same string. See Anal. p. 92; Calvin, Institutes 2.5.16. The second class offers a rich harvest to ignorance of Greek and Hebrew idioms, which has brought many monstrous errors into the Church. Let the well-worn trick serve as an example, Gen. 48.16: Jacob wished that his name be invoked over his children after his death. From this they infer that the dead can be invoked. It is a silly paralogism, which the ignorance of the Hebrew tongue produced, and of which the Papist teachers, men with keener noses, have themselves begun to be ashamed. See Anal. p. 213.

units.la: VIII. Fallacia compositionis fit, cùm conjunguntur dividenda.
units.tr: VIII. The fallacy of composition occurs when things that ought to be divided are joined together.

units.la: Luditur hoc Sophismate, vel ex natura rei, adeoque materia; vel dispositione sive rebus & verbis. De priori eleganter Dan. Elench.hæref.p.72. Quoties, quæ vel reipsa separari debent à se se, conjunguntur; vel quà ratione distingui oportet, confunduntur, atque inde fit fallacia, est à compositione. In quo nihil interest, si quæ in unum coagmentantur & connectuntur, reipsa & loco diduci possunt, sive non, veluti duo homines, qui sunt Individua, separari possunt: vel si animo tantùm & ratione distingui possunt, reipsa autem nequeant sejungi, veluti duæ in Christo naturæ, quæ separarari ipsa non possunt, quia in una persona unitæ sunt & coalescunt: ratione tamen distingui & discerni ni possunt. Quales item tres in Trinitate Personæ; qualia corpus & anima, & alia infinita, & omnia quidem quæ numero quidem unum dicuntur, distinguuntur tamen ratione. Posteriori modo fallacia compositionis committitur, quoties cunque à divisis ad conjuncta instituitur argumentatio, quod fit 1. in Enunciationibus modalibus, ut: possibile est ridentem lacrymare. Si enim participium ridentem referatur ad lacrymare, enunciatio erit falsa; sin cōjungatur cum modo Possibile, enunciatio est vera. Habet enim, qui modò ridet, facultatem etiam plorandi. 2. Cùm de toto colligitur, quod de partibus dicitur; ut: Duo & tria sunt par & impar. Quinq; sunt duo & tria. Ergò, quinq; sunt par & impar. 3. Cùm conjunguntur, quæ seorsim prædicantur, ut: Hic canis est pater. Hic canis est tuus. E Hic canis est pater tuus. Hujus fallaciæ etsi exempla Theologica plura afferri possent, unico tamen contenti, concomitantiæ, quam vocant, corporis & sanguinis in Missa infirmitatem ostendemus. Ita illi: Qui in cœna panem manducat, corpus Christi manducat. Corpus Christi non est sine sanguine suo. E qui in cœna panem manducat, corpus & sanguinem Christi manducat. Manifesta est hæc fallacia à compositione, & connexione separatorum. Separavit enim Christus carnem suam à sanguine suo. Calv. l. 4. Instit. c. 17. S. 18.
units.tr: This sophism is played upon either from the nature of the thing, and so from its matter, or from the arrangement, that is, from things and words. Of the former, Dan. writes elegantly in Elench. haeres. p. 72: Whenever things that ought to be separated from one another are joined together, or are confused where they ought to be distinguished, the fallacy arises from composition. In this it makes no difference whether the things that are fitted and connected into one can be separated in fact and place, or cannot, as two men, who are individuals, can be separated; or whether they can be distinguished only in mind and reason but cannot really be parted, as the two natures in Christ, which cannot be separated since they are united and joined in one person, yet can be distinguished and discerned in reason. Likewise the three Persons in the Trinity; likewise body and soul, and countless other things, indeed all those things which are said to be one in number and yet are distinguished in reason. The fallacy of composition is committed in the latter way whenever an argument proceeds from divided things to joined ones. This happens (1) in modal propositions, as: It is possible for the laughing man to weep. If the participle laughing is referred to weep, the proposition is false; but if it is joined with the modal word possible, the proposition is true, for the man who is now laughing has the capacity to weep as well. (2) When what is said of the parts is concluded of the whole, as: Two and three are even and odd. Five is two and three. Therefore five is even and odd. (3) When things predicated separately are joined together, as: This dog is a father. This dog is yours. Therefore this dog is your father. Although many theological examples of this fallacy could be cited, we shall be content with one, the weakness of the so-called concomitance of body and blood in the Mass. Thus they argue: He who eats bread at the supper eats the body of Christ. The body of Christ is not without its blood. Therefore he who eats bread at the supper eats the body and blood of Christ. This fallacy, arising from the composition and connection of things separated, is manifest. For Christ separated his flesh from his blood. Calv. l. 4 Instit. c. 17 S. 18.

units.la: IX. Fallacia divisionis est, quâ dividuntur conjungenda.
units.tr: IX. The fallacy of division is that by which things to be joined are divided.

units.la: Committitur hæc fallacia 1. in Enunciationibus, quarum partes conjunctione aliqua Grammatica conjunguntur, aut separantur, ut; omnis Christianus vel est Orthodoxus, vel Heterodoxus. At qui non omnis est Orthodoxus. E. omnis est Heterodoxus. Fallaciæ causa est majoris divisio, quæ tantùm vera est, si conjunctim sumatur, & ut simplex enuntiatio, cujus attributum Orthodoxus & Heterodoxus. 2. Cùm in majore nota quantitatis accepta collectivè, aut distributivè in genera singulorum, usurpata intelligitur distributivè, in singula generum; ut: DEUS vult omnes homines salvos fieri. Multi homines non fiunt salvi. E. multi homines,quos Deus vult fieri salvos,non fiunt salvi. Fallaciae sedes est in vocula omnis, quae, si de singulis generum accipiatur, majorem gignit falsam; si de generibus singulorum, minorem. 3. Cùm dictio,quę ad Antecedentia pertinet,ad consequentia refertur,aut contra. Tale est illud Menandri: ἐγὼ πε ἐθηκα ἆλον ὀν͂(α) ἐλεύθερον, quae verba, pro diversa interpunctione, diversum habent sensum. 4. Cùm locus aliquis citatur truncatè, exemplo Sathanae: Matth.c.4. 5. Cùm vox eadem,modò conjunctim sumitur,modo divisim: quae fallacia in sermone frequentius occurrit,quàm in scriptis,ubi εὐάλωτ@ καὶ ἀδύνατον ἐλεγχ@ est. 6. Cùm de partibus colligitur quod dicitur de toto. Septem sunt unus numerus. Tria & quatuor sunt septem. E. Tria & quatuor sunt unus numerus. 7. Cùm dividuntur,quae conjunctim praedicantur. Homerus est bonus Poeta. E. est bonus. Brevius. Fallacia divisionis committitur vel in simplici voce cùm per διαίρεσιν disjunguntur, quae ὑφ' ἓν, vel (συναίρεσις) conjungere deberet; vel in tota oratione. Sic quoties res conjunctae vel subjecto, cui in sunt; vel naturâ, quam habent, vel dicto seu oratione, separantur, hanc fallaciam constituunt: quae de re Dan. in Elench.haeref.p.81.82. Hac fallacia multis Papistae dogmatibus fucum faciunt,ea praesertim specie, qua loca Scripturae mutilant, eaque obtorto collo in obsequium ψευδεπιδᾶο καλῶν cogunt. Purgatorio subsidium quaerunt ex lem mate 1.Cor.3.13. καὶ ἑκάστου τὸ ἔργον ὁποῖόν ἐστι, τὸ πῦρ δοκιμάσει. E. est carcer purgatorius in quo poena peccatis debita eluitur. Limbo patrocinium ostendunt verbis Petri 1.Ep.3.v.19. ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξε. Pari felicitate Missam nuper quidam ex S. Sc. eruere voluit verbis. Missa est, inquit, calci Epistolarum Paulinarum attexitur. E. Missa vox ἀγραφ@ non est. Nec minus futile illud cujusdam pro dominio Cleri κλῆρος, quo dictum Christi, Luc.22. v.26. οἱ ἐξουσιάζοντες αὐτῶν εὐεργέται καλοῦνται, ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐχ οὕτως, vos autem non sic i.e. alia vero (usitato Hebraismo,cujusmodi occurrit Psal. 1.v.4.) vestri est ratio; scurriliter ita elusit: Vos autem non? Sic; Ex negativa affirmativam cudit. Hac etiam fallacia Transsubstantiationis portentum defendunt, & μλυτοπίας. Potest, inquiunt, DEUS sua efficere virtute, ut ex pane fiat corpus Christi. E. actu etiam fit. Separant hic voluntatem Dei à potentia, quae in rerum productione sunt ἀχωρίστα. Plura Deus potest, quàm vult.
units.tr: This fallacy is committed (1) in propositions whose parts are joined or separated by some grammatical conjunction, as: Every Christian is either Orthodox or Heterodox. But not every man is Orthodox. Therefore every man is Heterodox. The cause of the fallacy is the division of the major premise, which is true only if taken jointly and as a single proposition whose predicate is Orthodox and Heterodox. (2) When, in the major premise, a sign of quantity taken collectively or distributively into the kinds of individuals is understood distributively, into the individuals of the kinds, as: God wills all men to be saved. Many men are not saved. Therefore many men whom God wills to be saved are not saved. The seat of the fallacy lies in the little word all, which, if taken of the individuals of the kinds, produces a false major, and if taken of the kinds of individuals, a false minor. (3) When a word that belongs to the antecedent is referred to the consequent, or the reverse. Such is that saying of Menander: [ἐγὼ πε ἐθηκα ἆλον ὀν͂(α) ἐλεύθερον], words which, with a different punctuation, have a different sense. (4) When a passage is cited truncated, as in the example of Satan, Matth. 4. (5) When the same word is sometimes taken jointly and sometimes separately. This fallacy occurs more often in speech than in writing, where it is the phrase [εὐάλωτον καὶ ἀδύνατον ἐλέγχῳ], easily captured and impossible to refute. (6) When what is said of the whole is inferred of the parts. Seven is one number. Three and four are seven. Therefore three and four are one number. (7) When things predicated jointly are divided. Homer is a good poet. Therefore he is good. More briefly: the fallacy of division is committed either in a single word, when by division [διαίρεσις] things are separated which ought to be joined by synthesis [συναίρεσις] under one head, or in a whole discourse. Thus, whenever things joined together are separated, either from the subject in which they inhere, or from the nature they have, or from the statement or expression, they constitute this fallacy. Dan. treats of this at Elench. haeres. pp. 81, 82. By this fallacy the Papists lend colour to many of their doctrines, especially by the kind in which they mutilate passages of Scripture and twist them by force into the service of their [ψευδεπιδᾶο καλῶν]. They seek support for Purgatory from 1 Cor. 3.13: [καὶ ἑκάστου τὸ ἔργον ὁποῖόν ἐστι, τὸ πῦρ δοκιμάσει], and the fire shall try each man's work, of what sort it is. Therefore there is a purgatorial prison in which the punishment due to sins is washed away. They show support for Limbo from the words of 1 Pet. 3.19: [ἐν ᾧ καὶ τοῖς ἐν φυλακῇ πνεύμασι πορευθεὶς ἐκήρυξε], in which he went and preached to the spirits in prison. With equal success someone recently wished to extract the Mass from Holy Scripture by means of the words Missa est, he says, is appended to the end of the Pauline epistles. Therefore the word Mass is not [ἄγραφον], unwritten. No less frivolous is that man's argument for the dominion of the clergy [κλῆρος], by which he has mocked the saying of Christ, Luke 22.26: [οἱ ἐξουσιάζοντες αὐτῶν εὐεργέται καλοῦνται, ὑμεῖς δὲ οὐχ οὕτως], those who exercise authority over them are called benefactors, but you not so, that is, but with you it is otherwise (by the common Hebraism that occurs in Ps. 1.4). He scoffs: But you not so? Yes, so. He forges an affirmative out of a negative. By this same fallacy they defend the monstrosity of transubstantiation and their sophistry: God, they say, can by his power make the body of Christ out of bread; therefore it is actually done. They separate the will of God from his power, which in the production of things are inseparable. God can do more than he wills.

units.la: IX. Fallacia Figurae dictionis est, cùm, vel ex dictionum vel phrasium similitudine colligitur, eadem illis ac- cidentia, eundem sensum, aut significationem con- venire.
units.tr: IX. The fallacy of figure of speech occurs when it is inferred, from the similarity of words or phrases, that they have the same accidents, the same sense, or the same meaning.

units.la: Committitur ergò haec Fallacia, ὅταν τὸ μὴ τωυτὸν ὡσαύτως ἑρμηνεύεται, quando quis, quod idem non est, interpretatur eodem modo; ut loquitur Aristoteles, quod fieri solet. A. In vocibus 1. cùm ex similitudine terminationis colliguntur similia accidentia, vel Grammatica, vel Praedicamentalia, ut si quis diceret: Eustochium, cujus crebra apud Hieronymum mentio, generis esse neutrius; aut vapulare, erubescere, &c. pertinere ad Praedicamentum Actionis, quod terminatio faveat. 2. Cùm vocabula παρωνυμα seu Notiones secundae cum primis confunduntur, ut: Deus est ubiq.: ubiq. est adverbium. E. Deus est adverbium. 3. Cùm permiscentur res diversorum Praedicamentorum, ut: Quod mane in macello emisti, id in cœna comedisti: Atqui carnem crudam in macello emisti. E. Carnem crudam in cœna comedisti. Major de substantia carnis, Minor de Qualitate intelligitur. 4. Huc pertinent Sophismata, in quibus vocabula perperam junguntur cum Nominibus, Pronominibus, aut Adverbiis Relationis, qualis, quantus, qui, quae, quod, quot, toties, &c. ut: Quod ego sum, tu non es: Ego sum homo: Ergò tu non es homo. Assumitur hic species, cùm quod notet Individuum. B. Sed in tota oratione non uno modo hac peccari fallacia, docte observavit Danaeus in Elencho. Huc refert 1. Loca Scripturae, quae, cùm vel Imperium tantùm significent, parabolam, vel exemplum, ab una persona petitum, pro assertione, rei veritate, aut regula universali ponuntur. Ut, cùm ex verbis Scripturae; Fac bonum, fuge a malo, Psal. 34.15. concludunt: E. in
units.tr: This fallacy is committed when, as Aristotle puts it, "what is not the same is interpreted in the same way" [ὅταν τὸ μὴ τωυτὸν ὡσαύτως ἑρμηνεύεται], that is, when someone interprets in the same way what is not the same. A. In words: (1) when similar accidents, whether grammatical or predicamental, are inferred from similarity of ending, as if someone said that Eustochium, who is often mentioned by Jerome, is of neuter gender, or that vapulare, erubescere, &c. belong to the predicament of Action because the ending favours it. (2) When paronyms, or second notions, are confused with primary ones, as in: God is everywhere: "everywhere" is an adverb. Therefore God is an adverb. (3) When things of different predicaments are mixed up, as in: What you bought in the market in the morning, you ate at supper: but you bought raw meat in the market. Therefore: you ate raw meat at supper. The major is understood of the substance of the meat, the minor of its quality. (4) To this belong sophisms in which words are wrongly joined to nouns, pronouns, or relative adverbs such as qualis, quantus, qui, quae, quod, quot, toties, &c., as in: What I am, you are not: I am a man: therefore you are not a man. Here a species is assumed, since quod denotes an individual. B. But that this fault occurs in the whole discourse in more than one way has been learnedly observed by Daneau in his Elenchus. He refers here: (1) to passages of Scripture which, although they signify only a command, or a parable, or an example taken from one person, are put forward as an assertion, a statement of fact, or a universal rule. For example, when from the words of Scripture, Do good, depart from evil (Ps. 34:15), they conclude: therefore in

units.la: B nobis est vel bene vel male facere. Hujusmodi enim formulæ, quæ per Imperativum, & hypotheticum, ut vocant, modum concipiuntur, non tam notant, quid à nobis fieri possit, quàm quid fieri debeat. II. Hoc vitio laborant, qui literarum ordini & syllabarum, aut verborum situi ita religiosè sunt astricti, ut voces malint, quàm sensum venari. Ex hac officina prodit paralogismus: Johannes, Matth.3. 2. de pœnitentia hoc loquitur ordine: Pœnitentiam agite, quia appropinquat regnum cœlorum. E. Pœnitentia præcedit fidem, & internam mentis nostræ illuminationem. Vide Calvin.1.3.Instit.c.3.S.2. III. Altero extremo laborant, qui consequentiarum nobis cursum sistere aut sufflaminare conantur. Hic planè tumultuantur Veroniståe, quorum Methodista Veronius, modo omnes consequentiarum nexus tollit & jugulat, modo eas tantùm admittit, quæ faciunt ad stabiliendas partes Pontificias, non nostras: Vide Lect. Joh. Prideauxi, Lect.14. de usu Logices in Theologia, p.225. Sed quantum mutati à Majoribus suis, Doctoribus Scholasticis? Tantum abest (rectissimè observat idem) ut Scholastici hic dissentiant, ut Rationi plus quàm par est, (praxi saltem, si non thesi) attribuant. Receptissima sunt ista apud illos axiomata: 1. Theologiam esse argumentariam; Aq. Par.1.qua.1.art.8. 2. Distingui à fide, quia ut illa principia in sacris literis revelata apprehendit, ita hæc Conclusiones certas inde colligit. 3. Conclusionem, ex principio revelato & naturali, indubitatæ esse fidei. Nec de his fere (ut de cæteris) est aliqua inter illos altercatio. Horsum etiam tendunt Rodolphi Strodi, Richardi de Ferebrid, & Henrici Tisberg, spinosissimæ consequentiarum Regulæ, Sermonetæ commento Gaetani Monarchæ (ut appellatur) Philosophorum, declarationibus, & Antonii Frachantiani, & Pauli Pergulensis quæstionibus implicatissimis, auctæ potius, quàm illustratæ. Punctiores sunt ex hac parte Canus, Salmeron, Vasquez, Valentia, Albertinus, Pesantius, Kipa, Bannes & alii. Summatim ut dicam, inter locos in Theologia, unde solida deduci possunt argumenta, locum à Ratione Naturali, loco motum, à nullo ipsorum invenies. Quod postea & Campsani & Bellarmini de verbo Dei lib. Qui secus cum Methodistis ista sentiunt, quid moliuntur, nisi ut (quod Philistæi olim Samsoni) studiosis veritatis eruant oculos, vel unico saltem privent rationis lumine (quam obsessis propositi fœderis conditionem, Tyrannus ille Ammonita) quo contumeliosius omnes exponant omnium sannis & ludibriis? Ea media malunt, quæ, nisi ἀνεξετάστως admittantur, conclusionem pariunt ipsi vitæ & fortunæ insidiosam. Obsequium illi urgent, non rationes. Notum est illud Busdragi, Argolicensis Episcopi: Si quis Papam judicare velit, dices illi: O tu Ribalde, tu Pultrone, tu matto, quis tu es, ut tu Ecclesiam & Papam judicare velis? Tace, vel ego faciam tibi ignem ad culum, ut saltes sicut una pica: Ecclesia est Ecclesia, huic teneris obedire, vel combureris.
units.tr: us it is to do either well or ill. Formulas of this kind, which are framed in the imperative and in what they call the hypothetical mood, do not so much denote what can be done by us as what ought to be done. II. Those suffer from this vice who are so scrupulously bound to the order of letters, syllables, or the arrangement of words that they prefer to hunt down words rather than sense. From this workshop comes the paralogism: John, Matt. 3:2, speaks of repentance in this order: "Repent, for the kingdom of heaven is at hand." Therefore: repentance precedes faith and the inward illumination of our mind. See Calvin, Institutes 1.3, c. 3, s. 2. III. Those labour at the other extreme who try to halt or check the course of our consequences. Here the Veronians are in utter confusion, of whom Veronius the Methodist now destroys and strangles every connection of consequences, now admits only those which serve to establish Papist positions, not ours. See the lecture of John Prideaux, Lect. 14, on the use of logic in theology, p. 225. But how far have they departed from their elders, the Scholastic teachers? So far is it from the case (as the same man rightly observes) that the Scholastics disagree here, that they attribute to reason more than is fitting (in practice, if not in thesis). Those are most accepted axioms among them: 1. that theology is argumentative; Aquinas, Paris, 1, q. 1, art. 8. 2. that it is distinguished from faith, because, as faith grasps the principles revealed in Sacred Scripture, so theology gathers certain conclusions from them. 3. that a conclusion drawn from a revealed and a natural principle is of indubitable faith. Among them there is scarcely any dispute about these points (as about others). To this end also tend the most thorny rules of consequences of Rodolphus Strodus, Richard of Ferebrid and Henry of Tisberg, the declarations of the Sermoneta commentary by Gaetano the so-called Monarch of the Philosophers, and the most entangled questions of Antonio Frachantiano and Paolo of Pergola, which have been swollen rather than illuminated. More subtle on this side are Cano, Salmeron, Vásquez, Valentia, Albertinus, Pesantius, Kipa, Bannes and others. To put it briefly: among the topics in theology from which solid arguments can be drawn, you will find none moved from natural reason. What Campsanus and Bellarmine later said about the Word of God... Those who think otherwise than the Methodists, what are they striving for, unless (as the Philistines once did to Samson) to tear out the eyes of the lovers of truth, or at least to deprive them of the single light of reason (the condition which that Ammonite tyrant imposed on the besieged), so that they may expose everyone more insultingly to the mockery and derision of all? They prefer those means which, unless they are admitted without examination, bring about a conclusion treacherous to life and fortune itself. They press for obedience, not reasons. That saying of Busdragus, Bishop of Argos, is well known: If anyone wishes to judge the Pope, you will say to him: "O you rascal, you sot, you madman, who are you, that you wish to judge the Church and the Pope? Be quiet, or I will set fire to your backside so that you dance like a magpie: the Church is the Church; you are bound to obey her, or you will be burned."

units.la: X. Fallacia accentûs est, quâ pronunciantur eo- dem modo, quæ diversimodè scribuntur, aut pro- nunciantur diversimodè, quæ scribuntur eodem modo.
units.tr: X. The fallacy of accent is when words written in different ways are pronounced in the same way, or words written in the same way are pronounced in different ways.

units.la: Hoc ergo Sophisma bifariam committitur 1. Cùm scriptionis discrimen dissimulatur similitudine pronuntiationis, quod fit tribusmodis a. Cùm pronunciantur eodem modo, quæ variant literis. Crebrò hac fallacia peccatum est in versione LXX. viralì. Vide Thef.Philol.318. Sed & Muhammed turpissimè & planè pueriliter hic hallucinatus est. Vide lib.cit. p.125. Illi etiam, qui Nomina veteris Testamenti Latinè vel Græcè reddiderunt, per hanc fallaciam in multas abrepti sunt παραφυνεία. Vide Anal. P.1.p.323. b. Cùm fit deceptio ablatione necessariæ, & additione superfluæ aspirationis H. Est nonnunquam hic næyus in gente aliqua καθολικος. Lepidum est illud Catulli epigramma in Arrium quendam: Chommoda dicebat si quando commoda vellet Dicere, & Hinsidias Arrius Insidias. Et tum mirificè sperabat se esse locutum Cùm, quantum poterat, dixerat Hinsidias. Hoc maximè Sophismate Græcorum libri vetustiores, accentuum & Spirituum apicibus denudati, scatebant. Facile enim fuit pro ἐξ substituere, ἐξ, pro ἐν, ἐν, pro ἀν, ἀν. c. Referunt huc quidam malam totius orationis dispunctionem & distinctionem, in sua cola & membra, vel virgulis, vel punctis, adeoque falsam, & sensui mentiq; authoris contrariam alicujus sententiæ recitationem & pronuntiationem, sive sententia ea scripta sit, sive non. Ita Dan. El.p.50. Hujus tamen fallaciæ sedes propriamagis & propior videtur illa, quæ compositionis est & divisionis.
units.tr: This sophism is therefore committed in two ways. 1. When the difference of spelling is disregarded because of the similarity of pronunciation, which happens in three ways: a. when words that differ in letters are pronounced alike. This fallacy often led to error in the Septuagint, as in viralì. See Thef.Philol.318. Muhammed also blundered here most shamefully and quite childishly; see lib.cit. p.125. Those too who rendered the names of the Old Testament into Latin or Greek were carried off into many mistakes [παραφωνίας] through this fallacy. See Anal. P.1.p.323. b. When the deception comes from the removal of a necessary aspirate or the addition of a superfluous one, H. Sometimes this is a common blemish in some nation. There is a witty epigram of Catullus against a certain Arrius: he said Chommoda whenever he wished to say commoda (convenient), and Arrius said Hinsidias for Insidias (ambushes). And he hoped he had spoken wonderfully when he had said Hinsidias as loudly as he could. This sophism above all filled the older books of the Greeks, stripped of the marks of accents and breathings. For it was easy to put ἐξ for ἐξ [ex for ex], ἐν for ἐν [en for en], and ἀν for ἀν [an for an]. c. Some refer here the faulty punctuation and division of a whole sentence into its clauses and members, with commas or full stops, and so a false recitation and pronunciation of some saying, contrary to the sense and mind of the author, whether the saying was written that way or not. So Dan. El.p.50. Yet the proper and closer seat of this fallacy seems to be the one that concerns composition and division.

units.la: II. Secundi generis captiones duobus committuntur modis. a. Cùm, quæ vel ἐμφ... vel μιμητικῶς scripta sunt, accipiuntur quasi seria, aut contrà. Tale est illud Monachorum superstitiosorum. Omne quod Paulus monet, est faciendum: Monet Paulus, ne tangas, ne gustes, ne contrectes (Col.2.21.) Ergo non tangenda, non gustanda, non contrectanda quæ pereunt. b. Cùm syllabæ longæ, positæ pro brevibus, ipsam significationem mutant. Ita enim homonymiam, adeóque quatuor terminos, constituunt. Hac ludit fallacia, qui lepórem ponit pro lépore, &c. Et quanquam olim hæc se fallacia extenderit ad omnes voces, quantitate differentes, hodie tamen in sola penultima ostenditur.
units.tr: II. Captions of the second kind are committed in two ways. a. When things written either emphatically [ἐμφατικῶς] or mimetically [μιμητικῶς] are taken as if they were serious, or the reverse. Such is the saying of the superstitious monks: "Everything that Paul advises must be done." Paul advises: "Touch not, taste not, handle not" (Col. 2.21). Therefore things that perish are not to be touched, tasted, or handled. b. When long syllables, placed for short ones, change the meaning itself. For in this way they make a homonymy and so constitute four terms. This is the trick of the fallacy of one who takes the hare for the charm, and so on. And although this fallacy once extended to all words differing in quantity, today it is shown only in the penultimate syllable.

units.la: XI. Habuimus fallacias in dictione; Fallaciæ ex- tra dictionem sunt sequentes.
units.tr: XI. We have dealt with the fallacies in diction. The fallacies outside diction are the following.

units.la: XII. A. Fallacia Accidentis.
units.tr: XII. A. The Fallacy of Accident.

units.la: De hac fallacia varia Logicorum sunt judicia. Keckerm. Syst. Log. lib.3. p.569. Scribit, eam referri ad fallaciam, quæ est secundùm quid, sub qua continetur tanquam angustior sub latiori. Et ita non malè definitur Accidentis fallacia, quà medius terminus in una propositione per se intelligitur, in altera per accidens, ut; Quod movet seditiones, id adversatur societati humanæ. Evangelium movet seditiones. E. Evangelium adversatur societati humanæ. Burgersdicio Accidentis fallacia est, cùm colligitur subjecto convenire, quicquid de praedicato dicitur; quod duobus modis fieri ait; I. Cùm aliquid de attributo dicitur per accidens, ut; Homo est species: Socrates est homo. E. Socrates est species. Haec fallacia in eo sita est, quòd, esse speciem, de homine dicatur per Accidens; cùm hominem esse de Socrate dicatur per se. II. Cùm ipsum attributum de subjecto dicitur per Accidens; ut Mus rodit caseum. Mus est syllaba. E. Syllaba rodit caseum. Hic fallacia est, quia rodere caseum dicitur de mure per se, esse syllabam per accidens, ac ratione Nominis. Hanc tamen fallaciam alii ὀνόματος λέξεως tribuunt. Aliam Fallaciae Accidentis rationem, eámque intrinsecam seu internam ostendit, Dan. Elench.haeres. p.37. Fit, inquit, ex hoc Elencho fallacia, cùm non distinguitur inter id, quod de alio dicitur uti accidens, & illud quod de eodem enuntiatur uti Essentia, aut Essentiae pars. Essentia autem cuiusq; rei dicitur esse natura, quàres quaeq; constat, & quae definitione explicatur, veluti hominis Essentia est, animal rationale esse; fidei Essentia est, esse certissimam de Dei promissionibus erga nos per Christum fiduciam & cognitionem. Accidens cuiusq; rei est, quod ei adesse, vel ab ea abesse potest, vel saltem animo & mente fingi abesse, citra rei ipsius, de qua dicitur, interitum. Veluti in homine, album esse, doctum esse, sunt accidentia. In fideli & Christiano homine privatum, vel Magistratum esse, servum vel liberum, &c. Ergo, quod rei alicui inest velut accidens, sit tanquam Essentia eidem tribuitur, aut sumitur fit fallacia ab accidente. E.G. Sancti homines & Dei Prophetae per Sylvas errârunt, &c. E. qui hodie eadem faciunt sunt Sancti. Fallunt, inquit, ab Accidente. Neque enim haec definiunt veram Patrum sanctitatem, neq; de illa dicuntur tanquam Essentiae & definitionis ejus partes, sed tanquam Accidentia. Vera autem Patrum sanctitas in illo fuit, quòd & fidem DEI promissionibus habuerunt, & in ea fide toto vitae tempore perseverârunt. Huc potissimum refert fallaciam definitionis, cùm definitio falsa asseritur & affertur pro vera; ut, cùm concludunt Pontificii; Poenitentia sacra cinere, Jejunio & lachrymis fieri dicitur; Jes.7.6. E. poenitentia externis his partibus absolvitur. Sunt enim hæc Accidentia tantum Jejunii,non ipsa Essentia. Vide Calv. lib.3. Instit.c.3.S.17.
units.tr: Logicians disagree about this fallacy. Keckerm. Syst. Log. lib.3. p.569. writes that it belongs to the fallacy of "in a certain respect" (secundum quid), under which it is contained as the narrower under the wider. So the fallacy of accident is not badly defined as the case where the middle term is understood in one premise per se, and in the other per accidens, for example: What stirs up sedition is opposed to human society. The Gospel stirs up sedition. Therefore the Gospel is opposed to human society. Burgersdicius says that the fallacy of accident is when it is concluded that whatever is said of the predicate belongs to the subject, and he says this can happen in two ways: (1) when something is said of an attribute per accidens, for example: Man is a species. Socrates is a man. Therefore Socrates is a species. This fallacy lies in the fact that being a species is said of man per accidens, whereas being a man is said of Socrates per se. (2) when the attribute itself is said of the subject per accidens, for example: The mouse gnaws cheese. The mouse is a syllable. Therefore a syllable gnaws cheese. Here there is a fallacy, because gnawing cheese is said of the mouse per se, but being a syllable is said per accidens, and by reason of the name. Others, however, assign this fallacy to ὀνόματος λέξεως [onomatos lexeōs, the wording of a name]. Dan. Elench.haeres. p.37. shows another, and internal, account of the fallacy of accident. The fallacy arises from this refutation, he says, when no distinction is made between what is said of one thing as an accident and what is asserted of the same thing as its essence or a part of its essence. The essence of anything is its nature, by which it exists and which is explained by its definition. Thus the essence of man is to be a rational animal; the essence of faith is the most certain confidence and knowledge of God's promises toward us through Christ. An accident of anything is what can be present in it or absent from it, or at least be imagined in the mind to be absent, without the destruction of the thing of which it is said. Thus in a man, to be white, to be learned, are accidents. In a faithful and Christian man, to be a private person or a magistrate, a slave or free, and so on. Therefore, when what is present in a thing as an accident is attributed to it, or taken, as if it were its essence, a fallacy from accident arises. For example: Holy men and prophets of God have wandered in the woods, etc. Therefore those who do the same today are holy. They deceive, he says, by accident. For these things do not define the true holiness of the Fathers, nor are they said of it as its essence or parts of its definition, but as accidents. The true holiness of the Fathers lay in this, that they had faith in God's promises and persevered in that faith all their lives. To this he chiefly refers the fallacy of definition, when a false definition is asserted and offered as true; for example, when the Papists conclude: Sacred repentance is said to be effected by ashes, fasting and tears (Jes.7.6.). Therefore repentance is accomplished by these external parts. For these are only accidents of fasting, not its essence. See Calv. lib.3. Instit. c.3. §17.

units.la: B. Fallacia à dicto [a] secundum quid est, cùm ex præmissis, secundum quid veris, colligitur con- clusio simpliciter vera; Contrà, fallacia à dicto sim- pliciter est, cùm ex eo, quod simpliciter verum est, colligitur aliquid verum esse secundum quid.
units.tr: B. A fallacy from the dictum [a] in a certain respect occurs when a conclusion that is true without qualification is drawn from premises that are true only in a certain respect. Conversely, a fallacy from the dictum without qualification occurs when it is inferred from what is true without qualification that something is true only in a certain respect.

units.la: [a] Ita vocatur dictum, cujus Prædicatum subjecto convenit certo respectu, loco, & tempore. Quod Græci dicunt κατὰ τι κατηγορεῖσθαι. Simpliciter verò dictum est, cùm enunciatum toti subjecto & semper accommodari potest, vel cujus prædicatum subjecto convenit quovis respectu, parte, loco, &c. quod ἁπλῶς, κατὰ πάντα κατηγορεῖσθαι Græci exprimunt. Committitur fallacia à dicto secundum quid variis, maximè verò tribus modis. I. Ex quantitate, quæ vitiosè sumitur, cùm quod parti tantùm convenit, toti tribuitur; veluti, Æthiops habet albos dentes. E. Æthiops est albus. II. Cùm orationi adjecta est qualitas, quæ in conclusione postea omittitur, quod contingit si processus fiat à specie ad genus, à particulari ad universale, ut; Homo est animal rationale. E. omne animal est rationale. Paulus persecutus est Ecclesiam. E. omnes Apostoli. III. Cùm circumstantia temporis, loci, rei, personæ, Instrumenti, comparationis, modi, quæ orationi inest, conclusioni detrahatur. Temporis, ut; Ceremoniæ judaicæ Deo in V.T. placuerunt. E. & in Novo. Loci. Deus in V.T. gratiæ suæ sedem elegit Judæam. E. totum terrarum orbem. Rei & subjecti. Johannes Baptista præparabat vias Domini prædicans Verbum Dei. E. Johannes Baptista prædicabat eadem omnino, quæ postea Apostoli regnum Dei prædicantes. Personæ. Magistratui licet fontes gladio punire. E. & aliis. Instrumenti. Deus ordinariè nos alit pane. E. & absque pane. Modi. Qui petit & orat fide, impetrabit; E. qui petit & orat, impetrabit. IV. Cùm signum in rem ipsam transfertur, ut; Hæc statua est signum Dei. E. est Numen aliquod, seu quiddam cui Deus alligatus est. Atque ad hanc etiam fallaciam pertinet prava testimoniorum allegatio, quâ luxuriantem suam Theologiam Papistæ ubique onerant.
units.tr: [a] A dictum is so called when its predicate belongs to the subject in a certain respect, place, and time. The Greeks call this κατὰ τι κατηγορεῖσθαι [kata ti katēgoreisthai, predicated in some respect]. A dictum is taken without qualification when the statement can be applied to the whole subject and always, or when its predicate belongs to the subject in every respect, part, place, and so on; the Greeks express this as ἁπλῶς, κατὰ πάντα κατηγορεῖσθαι [haplōs, kata panta katēgoreisthai, predicated simply, in every respect]. The fallacy from the dictum in a certain respect is committed in various ways, but chiefly in three. (1) By quantity, which is wrongly taken when what belongs only to a part is attributed to the whole; for example, The Ethiopian has white teeth. Therefore the Ethiopian is white. (2) When a qualification has been added to the statement and is afterwards dropped in the conclusion. This happens when the inference proceeds from species to genus, or from particular to universal; for example, Man is a rational animal. Therefore every animal is rational. Paul persecuted the Church. Therefore all the Apostles did. (3) When a circumstance of time, place, thing, person, instrument, comparison, or manner, which is contained in the statement, is removed from the conclusion. Of time: The Jewish ceremonies were pleasing to God in the Old Testament. Therefore also in the New. Of place: In the Old Testament God chose Judea as the seat of his grace. Therefore the whole orb of the earth. Of thing and subject: John the Baptist prepared the ways of the Lord by preaching the Word of God. Therefore John the Baptist preached exactly the same things as the Apostles later, when they preached the kingdom of God. Of person: The magistrate may punish sinners with the sword. Therefore so may others. Of instrument: God ordinarily nourishes us with bread. Therefore without bread. Of manner: He who asks and prays in faith will obtain. Therefore he who asks and prays will obtain. (4) When a sign is transferred to the thing itself; for example, This statue is a sign of God. Therefore it is some divinity, or something to which God is bound. To this fallacy also belongs the perverse citation of testimonies, with which the Papists everywhere burden their luxuriant theology.

units.la: C. Ignoratio Elenchi est, quando vel planè tor- quetur & mutatur status [a] controversiæ; vel conclusio adversarii non directè opponitur [b] no- stræ thesi secundum Canones legitimæ oppositio- nis.
units.tr: C. Ignorance of the Refutation (Ignoratio Elenchi) occurs when either the state of the controversy is plainly twisted and changed, or the opponent's conclusion is not directly set against our thesis, as the rules of lawful opposition require.

units.la: [a] Alio nomine dicitur ἐπροζήτησις, καὶ μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος. Hâc crebrò chordâ oberrant Pontificii. Sic statum controversiæ subdolè detorquent, cùm in quæstione de Invocatione Sanctorum deflectunt ad quæstionem de Sanctis honorandis.
units.tr: This fallacy is also called [ἐπιζήτησις] and [μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος] (an irrelevant inquiry and a transition to another kind). The Papists often go astray on this point. They craftily twist the state of the controversy: when the question concerns the invocation of saints, they turn aside to the question of honouring the saints.

units.la: [b] Quod fit, cùm quæ sunt subordinata, finguntur opposita. Fontem hujus fallaciæ Danæus clarè & perspicuè ita detegit. Elench.hæref.p.144. Ergo quoties quædam de uno aliquo & eodem dicuntur non una tamen & eadem ratione, sed diversa, (quæ in conclusione tamen ponuntur, tanquam eadem ratione & secundum idem, & similiter dicta essent) fit fallacia ex hoc loco, qui dicitur Ignoratio Elenchi. Sensus enim diversitatem confundit ea ratio, & diversarum rerum considerationem miscet, quæ fieri & distingui debebat. Ex quo fit, ut multis modis ex hoc loco fallacia committatur. Nam sive divina cum humanis confundantur, sive allegoriæ inutiles invehantur, & sensus scripturæ incertus, sive aliud mens authoris velle, aliud autem verba ipsa orationis significare videantur, sive diversus rerum respectus & diversa dicti ratio non observetur, atq; inde fiat committatur q. fallacia, pertinet ad hunc locum; denique omnis fraudis faciendæ modus inquo ratio diversitatis vel non intelligitur, vel non observata est. E.G. Deus nos jubet ista facere, illa evitare, ad eaque nos exhortatur. E. ista facere, & illa evitare nos posse declarat; idque per nos ipsos; hanc struì fallaciam censet. Neq; enim hanc mentem esse Scripturæ, dum nos ad bene vivendum exhortatur, ut doceat, quid ipsi per nos facere possimus; sed ut intelligamus quantum debeamus, & quanta sit nostra imbecillitas; Cal. lib. 3. Instit. c 17. S. 1. 2.
units.tr: This happens when things that are subordinate are made to appear opposed. Danaeus lays bare the source of this fallacy clearly and plainly (Elench. hæref., p. 144): Therefore, whenever certain things are said of one and the same subject, but not in one and the same respect, and yet in the conclusion they are put as if they were said in the same respect and in the same way, a fallacy arises from this topic, which is called Ignorance of the Refutation. For this confusion of meaning mixes the consideration of different things which ought to be kept apart and distinguished. Hence the fallacy is committed in many ways from this topic: whether divine things are confused with human, or useless allegories are introduced, and the sense of Scripture is left uncertain; or whether the author's mind seems to will one thing while the words themselves signify another; or whether the different respects of things and the different sense of what is said are not observed, and so a fallacy is committed. In short, every mode of deceit in which the difference of respect is either not understood or not observed belongs to this topic. For example: God commands us to do these things and avoid those, and exhorts us to them. Therefore he declares that we are able to do these things and avoid those, and this through ourselves. Danaeus judges that this fallacy is constructed here. For it is not the mind of Scripture, when it exhorts us to live well, to teach what we can do by ourselves; rather it wants us to understand how much we owe and how great our weakness is (Calvin, Institutes, bk. 3, ch. 17, §§ 1, 2).

units.la: D. Petitio [a] Principii est, cùm nullo medio adhibi- to conclusio repetitur, vel [b] iisdem, vel [c] æ- quipollentibus verbis, aut cùm controversum probatur per [d] æquè controversum. Vocatur aliâs [e] Demonstratio Circularis.
units.tr: D. Begging the Question (Petitio Principii) occurs when the conclusion is repeated with no middle term introduced, either in the same words or in equivalent ones, or when what is disputed is proved by means of something equally disputed. It is otherwise called Circular Demonstration.

units.la: [a] Trita est hæc & usitata fallaciæ ἐπιγεαφὴ, quam tamen vitiosam esse docti viderunt. Burgersd. l. 2. p. 373. Hoc Sophisma vulgò dictum petitio principii, cùm sit petitio ejus, quod in principio quæsitum fuit. Dan. Elench. pag. 117. Ut facilius locus ipse & ratio fallaciæ quæ fit, indicetur, inscriptio hujus Elenchi sic fieri debebit; Sumere id, de quo primùm controvertebatur. Nam si verè loqui volumus, & Mathematicorum more, nihil habet vitii in se petitio principii. Cùm sint enim in quaq; arte principia indemonstrabilia, peti atq; postulari debent, ut concedantur. Et rectè id fit, non autem vitiosè: Unde nata sunt illa, quæ in Geometria & apud Euclidem αἰτήματα, id est: petitiones, sive postulata, appellantur, & rectâ Methodo & rationi artium & scientiarum tradendarum convenienter illud fit. Quod si hic locus inscribendus esset, Petere principium, dixissent Græci αἰτεῖν ἀρχὴν, non autem sic, λαμβάνειν τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ.
units.tr: This fallacy, a commonplace and familiar one, has been rightly seen by learned men to be faulty. Burgersdijk (bk. 2, p. 373): This sophism, commonly called begging the question, is a request for that which was sought at the start. Danaeus (Elench., p. 117): So that the place itself and the reason of the fallacy that arises may be more easily indicated, the title of this refutation should be written thus: taking as granted that very thing which was first in dispute. For if we wish to speak truly, and in the manner of the mathematicians, begging the question has nothing faulty in itself. For in every art there are first principles that cannot be demonstrated, and these must be asked for and requested so that they may be granted. This is done rightly and not faultily; hence those things which in geometry and in Euclid are called [αἰτήματα], that is, requests or postulates, arose, and this is done in accordance with the right method and the nature of teaching the arts and sciences. But if this topic were to be titled as a fallacy, the Greeks would have said [αἰτεῖν ἀρχὴν] (to ask for a beginning), not [λαμβάνειν τὸ ἐν ἀρχῇ] (to take what is at the beginning).

units.la: [b] Cujus tamen fallaciæ, tanquam nimis apertæ, nullam habendam rationem docti censent. Nisi enim mutetur vel subjecti, vel Prædicati nomen, mera committitur & nugatoria ταυτολογία, quam κακκυσμὸν vocant: ut; Ecclesia Romana est Catholica, quia est Catholica.
units.tr: Learned men judge, however, that no account should be taken of this fallacy, since it is too obvious. Unless either the name of the subject or of the predicate is changed, it is a bare and trifling tautology, which they call [κακκυσμός] (idle repetition), for example: The Roman Church is Catholic, because it is Catholic.

units.la: [c] Ita peccant Pontificii circa ἀναμαρτησίαν sui Papæ. Qui circa doctrinam fidei non potest errare, ille est ἀναμάρτητος. Pontifex circa doctrinam fidei non potest errare. Ergò, &c.
units.tr: The Papists err in this way concerning the impeccability [ἀναμαρτησία] of their Pope: whoever cannot err concerning the doctrine of faith is [ἀναμάρτητος] (sinless). The Pope cannot err concerning the doctrine of faith. Therefore, etc.

units.la: Hoc sophismate in Theologia Pontificia nihil crebrius est. Dixeris hanc βάσιν penè esse totius Papatus. Nam & ex Patrum authoritate & consuetudine Ecclesiæ, in eminentissimo fori Theologici throno collocatis, patrocinium pollicentur Invocationi sanctorum, Purgatorio, aliisque dogmatibus ἀγεά-φοις καὶ καταγεάφοις. Tale est: Petrus est Apostolorum Princeps non ordine tantùm, sed & Imperio. E. & Papa Romanus. Soli Petro commissæ sunt claves regni cælorum. E. Solius Papæ est Oecumenica Ecclesia ἐπισκοπή. Patres invocarunt Sanctos. E. Sancti sunt invocandi. Septenarius sacramentorum numerus ab universa receptus est Ecclesia Romana. E. ab eo non recedendum, &c.
units.tr: There is nothing more frequent in Papal theology than this sophism. One might say that this [βάσις] (basis) is almost the whole of Papacy. For they promise patronage, both from the authority of the Fathers and from the custom of the Church, to the invocation of saints, to Purgatory, and to other dogmas [ἀγράφοις καὶ καταγράφοις] (unwritten and written), set on the most eminent throne of theological judgment. The argument runs thus: Peter is prince of the Apostles not only in order but also in authority; therefore the Roman Pope is too. The keys of the kingdom of heaven were committed to Peter alone; therefore the oversight [ἐπισκοπή] of the ecumenical Church belongs to the Pope alone. The Fathers invoked the saints; therefore the saints are to be invoked. The septenary number of the sacraments has been received by the whole Roman Church; therefore we must not depart from it, etc.

units.la: Nomenclaturæ hujus rationem paulò altius repetimus. Circulus, ab antiquo circuendo dictus, est reciproca probatio, quâ unū ex altero colligitur & demonstratur. Vocatur aliâs demonstratio vel probatio Cyclica, orbicularis, circulus Philosophicus, probatio κύκλῳ, ἀπόδειξις κυκλοειδής. Consideratur autem materialiter in Propositionibus convertibilibus, quæ ipsum circulum ingrediuntur; & formaliter in Syllogismo Apodictico, cùm propositio dubia per conclusionem & alteram propositionem conversam confirmatur. Usus & finis ratione, appositè circulus distinguitur in Logicum & Sophisticum. Logicus, vel duos habet Syllogismos, vel plures. Ille ea probandi ratio est, quæ, facta demonstratione τῶν ὅτι, primum per effectum demonstrat causam: Examine deinde instituto, demonstratione τῷ διότι per causam demonstrat effectum. Neque enim huc tantùm circularis hæc demonstratio facit, ut veritas confirmetur propositionis conversæ (si enim conclusio ex utraque præmissa est certa, propositioni conversæ fidem faciunt) sed etiam ut regressui inserviat ab effecto ad causam; seu conversioni demonstrationis τῶν ὅτι in demonstrationem τῷ διότι, dum ex notiore effecto causa ignota cognoscitur & intelligitur, & ex causa jam nota, effectus deducitur. Unde & Regressus, de quo peculiar. scripsit lib. Zabarella, vocatur. Ita autem Syllogismus unus ex altero efficitur, ut cùm; vera existente conclusione; non necesse sit veras esse præmissas, sicque negetur Major; tunc conclusio prioris Syllogismi stamatur loco propositionis in posteriore Syllogismo, quæ combinata cum altera propositione conversa, eam dabit conclusionem, quæ fuit propositio Syllogismi prioris. V.G. Ex Syllogismo sequenti; Omnes justificati pacem habent cum Deo. At omnes verè credentes sunt justificati. E. Omnes verè credentes pacem habent cum Deo; talis instituitur probatio circularis: Omnes verè credentes pacem habent cum Deo. At omnes justificati sunt verè credentes. E. Omnes justificati pacem habent cum Deo. Quòd si minorem neget adversarius, Regressus ita instituendus, ut Propositio major convertatur simpliciter, conclusio in assumtionem migret, & assumtio in conclusionem, quæ circularis demonstrationis facilima est ratio, ut: Quicunq; habet pacem conscientiæ, ille habet certam fiduciam remissionis peccatorum. Omnis justificatus habet pacem conscientiæ. E. Omnis justificatus habet certam fiduciam remissionis peccatorum. Demonstratio hæc τῶ̃ν in demonstratione τῶ̃ν transit hoc modo: Qui habet certam fiduciam remissionis peccatorum, ille habet pacem conscientiæ. Omnis justificatus habet certam fiduciam remissionis peccatorum. E. Omnis justificatus habet pacem conscientiæ. De circulo Logico plures habente Syllogismos, quorum ille dicitur perfectus, quòd sex; hic imperfectus, quòd paucioribus absolvitur syllogismis, commentandi locus non est. Videatur Jul. Pac. in II. Anal. Post. c. 5. p. 312. Ad Sophisticum, qui hujus propriè loci est, accedimus, seu ἄλογον, qui aliud nihil est, quàm puerilis principii petitio, quâ progressus fit in infinitum, & aliquid per se ipsum, dubium per æquè dubium, circulo & ambitu in se se recurrente, probatur. Estque vel manifestus vel Crypticus. Ille κατάφωρον primo statim intuitu deprehenditur; hic ita involvitur, ut nonnisi accurata instituta analysi se prodat, perinde ut serpens in gyrum se volvens, ita ut nec cauda appareat, nec caput. Hujusmodi circulo, tanquam Diogenis dolio rotantur Pontificii, tum aliàs, tum verò maximè in nobilissima illa quæstione: Unde constet nobis de divina S. Sc. authoritate? Respondent illi, eam constare testimonio infallibili Ecclesiæ. Si quæratur; Unde pendeat hoc Ecclesiæ testimonium? regerunt: Ex eo quòd Ecclesia sit columna & stabilimentum veritatis. Si instes: unde veritas hujus promissi; Iterum ad testimonium Ecclesiæ infallibile confugiunt; & sic chordâ semper oberrant eadem. Purgare se conantur ab hac ludicra argumentatione Jesuitæ, Gregorius de Valentia, Gretserus & Becanus, hic cumprimis, qui tractatu peculiari de circulo Calvinistico, argumentationis hujus ruditatem & absurditatem declinare voluit. Sed frustra. Omnia examinare non licet. Becani paucis perstringemus κρησφύγετον. Negat, suos Sophisticum committere circulum; sed salsissima nixus suppositione. Suppono, inquit, ex Philosophia circulum tunc committi, quando hoc per illud, & illud vicissim per hoc probamus, apud eum, qui neutrum concedit & æquè de utroq; dubitat. Has si φλυαρίας nostri proferrent, ipsis tyronibus ludibrium deberent. Quis unquam petitionem principii, quæ aliud nihil est, quàm lusus κυκλοδίης, ad has leges astrinxit? Satis est, obscurum aut controversum per æquè aut magis obscurum & controversum probari, non requiritur medium teminum esse & formaliter & materialiter dubium. V.G. Pontificius, demonstraturus sui Papæ ἀναμαρτησίαν, medio termino utitur; Quia hanc ei Scriptura adjudicat. Nego hanc minorem. Affertur, probationis loco, textus Matth.16. Tu es Petrus, &c. Atque hic quidem locus ἀνεξαγώνιος est, de ejus quippe authoritate nemo dubitat Christianus; sed quia malè ad probandam quæstionem adhibetur, causa existit argumentationi circulari hoc modo: Papa non potest errare, cur? quia ei porta inferorum non possunt prævalere. Porta inferorum Papæ non prævalent, cur? quia non errat. Nunc ex alio capite, inquit Jesuita, ostendam, nos circulo non includi. Res ita habet. Aliud est loqui de fide seu, fidei assensu secundùm se, aliud de acceptatione fidei. Unde potest institui duplex quæstio, & duplex resolutio. Altera de causa fidei secundùm se, ut si quæram; quare certò & infallibiliter credis articulos in Symbolo comprehensos? Respondebo; quia Deus revelavit. Altera de causa acceptationis fidei, ut si quæro, quid te impulit aut permovit ut in animum induceres credere articulos tam obscuros, & humanum captum excedentes? Respondebo; authoritate Ecclesiæ & consensu fidelium. Sed λόγοι sunt & verborum fumi. I. Non dicimus omnem argumentationem vel esse circularem; vel omnem circularem esse nugatoriam. Fides, quæ se resolvit in revelationem Dei, factam per scripta Prophetarum & Apostolorum, recte procedit. Quæ vero in Ecclesiæ authoritate recumbit & altius non assurgit, ab hoc Sophistico circulo eximi non potest, quod non tantum fit ratione acceptationis; sed etiam secundum se: Quanquam non cujusvis sit Idiotæ, has capere subtilitates. Exemplo sit Carbonarius ille, cujus fidem & factum Hosius Cardinalis, cum aliis, laudat. Quid credis, quærit Diabolus? Quod Ecclesia credit, respondet carbonarius. Quid ergo, reponit Satan, credit Ecclesia? Id ipsum respondet Carbonarius, quod ego credo. Ab hac thesi si descendatur ad hypothesin, circulus, in ipsa etiam acceptatione fidei palam emerget. Talem enim habemus à Carbonario resolutionem. Cur credis Papam esse Oecumenicum Episcopum? Resp. Quia idem credit Ecclesia. Cur Ecclesia credit? Jam hic vel ad authoritatem Ecclesiæ, quia sic ei placuerit, vel ad Scripturæ verba, provocabitur. Si illud; circulus est Sophisticus: Si hoc, iterum vel circularis erit argumentatio, dum verbis minimè huc pertinentibus τὸ ζητούμενον probatur; vel turpissima παρεχμηνεία. Certum est omnia tandem in Ecclesiæ authoritatem resolvi.
units.tr: We repeat the reason for this name a little more fully. Circle (circulus), named from the old verb circuendo, "going round," is reciprocal proof, by which one thing is inferred and demonstrated from another. It is also called demonstration or proof cyclical, orbicular, philosophical circle, proof in a circle [κύκλῳ], circular demonstration [ἀπόδειξις κυκλοειδής]. It is considered materially in convertible propositions, which make up the circle itself, and formally in an apodictic syllogism, when a doubtful proposition is confirmed through the conclusion and the other proposition converted. By its use and purpose, the circle is aptly divided into logical and sophistical. The logical circle has two syllogisms, or more. It is the method of proof which, once demonstration that [τῶν ὅτι] has been made, first demonstrates the cause through the effect; then, when the inquiry is set up, demonstrates the effect through the cause by demonstration why [τῷ διότι]. For this circular demonstration does not serve only to confirm the truth of the converted proposition (if the conclusion is certain from each premise, they make the converted proposition credible), but also serves the regress from effect to cause, or the conversion of demonstration that into demonstration why: from the better-known effect the unknown cause is known and understood, and from the cause now known the effect is deduced. Hence it is also called Regress, on which Zabarella wrote a special book. One syllogism is made from another in such a way that, when the conclusion is true, the premises need not be true, and so the major is denied. Then the conclusion of the first syllogism takes the place of the proposition in the second syllogism, which, combined with the other converted proposition, gives the conclusion that was the proposition of the first syllogism. For example, from the following syllogism: All justified persons have peace with God. But all who truly believe are justified. Therefore all who truly believe have peace with God. A circular proof is set up thus: All who truly believe have peace with God. But all justified persons are true believers. Therefore all justified persons have peace with God. If the opponent denies the minor, the regress is to be set up so that the major proposition is converted simply, the conclusion passes into the assumption, and the assumption into the conclusion. This is a very easy form of circular demonstration, as follows: Whoever has peace of conscience has a certain confidence in the forgiveness of sins. Every justified person has peace of conscience. Therefore every justified person has a certain confidence in the forgiveness of sins. This demonstration passes into demonstration why in this way: Whoever has a certain confidence in the forgiveness of sins has peace of conscience. Every justified person has a certain confidence in the forgiveness of sins. Therefore every justified person has peace of conscience. Concerning the logical circle, which has several syllogisms, of which one is called perfect because it is completed with six, and another imperfect because it is completed with fewer syllogisms, this is not the place to comment. See Jul. Pac. on the Second Posterior Analytics, chapter 5, p. 312. We come to the sophistical circle, which properly belongs to this place, or the "without reason" [ἄλογον], which is nothing other than a childish begging of the principle, by which progress is made to infinity, and something is proved through itself, a doubtful thing through an equally doubtful thing, the circle running back on itself in a round course. It is either manifest or cryptic. The former is caught at once at first glance [κατάφωρον]; the latter is so wrapped up that it reveals itself only on careful analysis, just as a serpent coiling into a ring shows neither tail nor head. The Papists turn round in such a circle, like Diogenes' tub, both elsewhere and above all in that most noble question: How do we know for certain the divine authority of Holy Scripture? They answer: it is established by the infallible testimony of the Church. If asked, On what does this testimony of the Church depend? they reply: From the fact that the Church is the pillar and ground of truth. If you press further, whence the truth of this promise? they again take refuge in the infallible testimony of the Church, and so they always wander on the same string. The Jesuits, Gregory of Valencia, Gretser and Becanus, try to purge themselves of this childish argument, Becanus above all, who in a special treatise on the Calvinist circle wished to avoid the crudeness and absurdity of this argument. But in vain. We cannot examine everything. We shall briefly strike Becanus's refuge. He denies that his people commit a sophistical circle, but leans on a most silly supposition. "I suppose," he says, "that a circle is committed in philosophy when we prove this by that, and that by this in turn, before one who concedes neither and doubts both equally." If our people put forward such nonsense, they would deserve mockery even from beginners. Who ever bound begging the question, which is nothing other than a play of circular trickery, to these rules? It is enough that the obscure or disputed is proved by what is equally or more obscure and disputed; it is not required that the middle term be doubtful both formally and materially. For example, the Papist, wishing to demonstrate the infallibility of his Pope, uses a middle term: Because Scripture adjudges this to him. I deny this minor. As proof is brought the text Matt. 16, You are Peter, etc. This place is indeed beyond dispute, for no Christian doubts its authority; but because it is badly applied to prove the question, there arises a circular argument in this way: The Pope cannot err; why? Because the gates of hell cannot prevail against him. The gates of hell do not prevail against the Pope; why? Because he does not err. "Now from another angle," says the Jesuit, "I will show that we are not included in a circle. The matter stands thus. It is one thing to speak of faith, or the assent of faith, in itself, and another of the acceptance of faith. Hence a twofold question and a twofold answer can be set up. One concerns the cause of faith in itself: if I ask, why do you believe the articles contained in the Creed certainly and infallibly? I answer, because God has revealed them. The other concerns the cause of the acceptance of faith: if I ask, what impelled or moved you to bring yourself to believe articles so obscure and beyond human grasp? I answer, by the authority of the Church and the consent of the faithful." But these are words and smoke. I. We do not say that every argument is circular, or that every circular argument is futile. Faith which resolves itself into the revelation of God, made through the writings of the prophets and apostles, proceeds rightly. But faith which rests on the authority of the Church and does not rise any higher cannot escape this sophistical circle, since it is so not only by reason of acceptance but also in itself; although it is not for every layman to grasp these subtleties. Take as an example that charcoal-burner whose faith and deed Cardinal Hosius, among others, praises. "What do you believe?" asks the devil. "What the Church believes," answers the charcoal-burner. "What then," replies Satan, "does the Church believe?" The charcoal-burner answers: "The very thing I believe." If we descend from this thesis to the hypothesis, the circle will plainly appear even in the acceptance of faith itself. For we have such a resolution from the charcoal-burner: Why do you believe the Pope to be the ecumenical bishop? Answer: Because the Church believes the same. Why does the Church believe it? Here one will be referred either to the authority of the Church, because it has so pleased it, or to the words of Scripture. If the former, the circle is sophistical; if the latter, the argument will again be either circular, while the matter to be proved is proved by words not pertaining here at all, or else a most shameful misinterpretation. It is certain that everything is at last resolved into the authority of the Church.

units.la: II. Motiva seu media acceptationis fidei, nulla alia admittuntur, quàm quæ Ecclesia tradit, quæ probat & adhibet. Ita quidem verba expectent sine re, qui vel hilum ullis mediis, absque authoritate Ecclesiæ, tribuunt.
units.tr: II. The motives or means of accepting faith admit of no others than those which the Church hands down, which it proves and employs. Indeed, those who ascribe the least force to any means apart from the authority of the Church would be expecting words without substance.

units.la: E. Fallacia consequentis est, cùm aliqua enuntiatio ex altera colligitur, ex qua non sequitur: vel; quando Major Syllogismi propositio nullum aut vitiosum nexum habet, seu consequentiam. Vocatur aliàs σόφισμα ὡς ἐπόμενον, & ἀνακόλουθία.
units.tr: E. The fallacy of the consequent occurs when a proposition is inferred from another from which it does not follow; or when the major premise of a syllogism has no connection with the conclusion, or a faulty one. It is also called the sophism "as following" [σόφισμα ὡς ἐπόμενον] and anacoluthia [ἀνακόλουθία].

units.la: Latè hoc Sophisma vagatur, & committitur, vel in materia, vel in forma. Forma hàc fallacià laborat, quoties leges Syllogisticæ vel generales violantur, vel speciales. Quot modis in materia hic peccetur, dici vix potest. Nobis aliquot dedisse satis erit errorum sedes. Est ergò fallacia consequentis. I. Cùm non est parpartium sufficiens enumeratio. Ut si quis argumentetur : In Juda Iscariota pœnitentia habemus contritionem cordis, confessionem oris, satisfactionem operis. E. Pœnitentia ejus fuit vera ; committit fallac. conseq. propter insufficientem membrorum enumerationem, deest enim fides. II. Cùm conjugatorum natura, non rectè intellecta, in hanc impellimur fraude V. G. Si quis concludat : Hic somnum capit. E. est Somniculosus. Fallit à non consequenti, quia hæc duo non sunt Conjugata Logica. Vel; Qui facit Justitiam, Justus est, adeóq; attributum DEI communicabile participat : Ergò qui miracula patrat, quod proprie DEI est, potens vel omnipotens est. III. Cùm à minori ad majus, vel à genere ad speciem affirmativè aliquid concluditur. Ut; Sancti sunt honorandi. E. & invocandi. Conjugium est mysterium E. & Sacramentum. IV. Ubi illud sumitur, quod nullo modo consequens est. Ejusmodi asyllogistiæ obviæ sunt apud Pontificios. Ut ; Decimæ sunt solvendæ. E. Per quadraginta dies est jejunandum. Quod quidem argumentum Gregorii est. Plura exempla dedimus in ὁδηγῷ P.1.p.198. Alii quatuor regulas in illatione consequentis, ex antecedente observandas commendant, quarum una si violetur, nulla erit consecutio. Prima regula: Universalis affirmans non convertitur simpliciter. Non ergo valet : Omnis adulator blandus est. E. omnis blandus adulator. II. Ex universali affirmante non colligitur universalis negans, nisi per contrapositionem. Nihil ergo efficitur : Quicquid genitum est, habet principium. E. quod non est genitum, ut anima humana, mundus, non habet principium ; sed per contrapositionem : E. quod non habet principium, non est genitum. III. Minor non debet esse negata in prima figura, seu, quod eodem redit : Ex remotione antecedentis non potest colligi remotio consequentis. Non valet ergo : Omnis homo est animal. Equus non est homo. E. neque animal. IV. Altera præmissarum debet esse negata in secunda Figura, sive, Non debet positio antecedentis colligi, ex positione consequentis. Decipitur ergo captione consequentis sequenti syllogismo. Omnis adulator est blandus. Crispus est blandus. E. Crispus est adulator.
units.tr: This sophism wanders widely and is committed either in the matter or in the form. The form is faulty whenever the general or special rules of syllogism are violated. The ways in which one may err in matter can hardly be stated. It will be enough to give a few sources of error. This is the fallacy of the consequent. (1) When the enumeration of parts is not sufficient. For example, if someone argues: In Judas Iscariot we find repentance: contrition of heart, confession of mouth, satisfaction of work. Therefore his repentance was true. He commits the fallacy of the consequent through an insufficient enumeration of the parts, for faith is missing. (2) When the nature of conjugates is not rightly understood, we are driven into this deception. For example, if someone concludes: He falls asleep. Therefore he is sleepy. He falls into the fallacy of the non-consequent, because these two are not logical conjugates. Or: He who does justice is just, and so shares in the communicable attribute of God. Therefore he who works miracles, which belongs properly to God, is powerful or omnipotent. (3) When something is affirmatively concluded from the lesser to the greater, or from the genus to the species. For example: Saints are to be honoured. Therefore they are to be invoked.
