Marriage is a mystery. Therefore it is a sacrament. (4) When that is taken as a consequence which in no way follows. Such non-sequiturs are common among the Papists. For example: Tithes are to be paid. Therefore one must fast for forty days. This argument is indeed Gregory's. We have given more examples in the Hodegus [ὁδηγῷ], part 1, page 198. Others recommend four rules to be observed in drawing a consequence from an antecedent, and if any one of them is violated, there will be no valid inference. First rule: A universal affirmative does not convert simply. So this does not hold: All flatterers are smooth-tongued. Therefore all smooth-tongued men are flatterers. Second: A universal negative is not inferred from a universal affirmative, except by contraposition. So nothing follows from: Whatever is begotten has a beginning. Therefore what is not begotten, such as the human soul or the world, has no beginning. But by contraposition: What has no beginning is not begotten. Third: The minor premise must not be negative in the first figure; or, what comes to the same thing: From the denial of the antecedent no denial of the consequent can be inferred. So this does not hold: Every man is an animal. A horse is not a man. Therefore it is not an animal. Fourth: One of the premises must be negative in the second figure; or, the positing of the antecedent must not be inferred from the positing of the consequent. Hence one is deceived by the seduction of the consequent in the following syllogism: All flatterers are smooth-tongued. Crispus is smooth-tongued. Therefore Crispus is a flatterer.

units.la: F. Fallacia à non causa ut causa est, quando ad pro- bandam conclusionem assumitur falsa causa.
units.tr: F. The fallacy of taking a non-cause as a cause occurs when a false cause is assumed in order to prove the conclusion.

units.la: Huic quidem fallaciæ latissimi à nonnullis conceduntur limites: Nescio tamen, an satis ἀκριβῶς. His verò causa non tantùm est, à quo pendet causatum; sed in genere omnis medius terminus. Hinc ab aliis vocatur falsi medii assumtio. Quo referunt omnia argumenta, quæ, ut vulgò dicunt, desumuntur à baculo ad angulum. Quæ tamen commodius ad alias fallaciarum classes pertinent, eam præsertim quæ est consequentis. Ergò dicimus, Fallaciam hanc committi vel in Syllogismo ducente ad absurdum, vel in Syllogismo directo. Illius exemplum sit. Omne immortale est absolutè æternum. Anima est immortalis. E. anima est æterna. Atquihæc conclusio est falsa; quæ ex majori falsò in fertur. Hujus verò species sunt variæ.
units.tr: Some have set very wide limits to this fallacy, though I do not know whether they are sufficiently accurate [ἀκριβῶς]. For these writers, a cause is not only that on which the thing caused depends, but in general any middle term. Hence others call it the assumption of a false middle. To this belong all the arguments which, as people commonly say, are drawn from the staff to the corner. These, however, belong more conveniently to other classes of fallacies, especially to that of the consequent. We say, therefore, that this fallacy is committed either in a syllogism leading to the absurd, or in a direct syllogism. An example of the former: Everything immortal is absolutely eternal. The soul is immortal. Therefore the soul is eternal. But this conclusion is false, and it is inferred from a false major premise. There are various kinds of this fallacy.

units.la: I. Cùm causis per accidens tribuitur, quod non convenit nisi causis per se. Quo faciunt perplexitas, & abusus. Ex lectione Scripturæ natæ sunt hæreses. E. Laicis non est legenda.
units.tr: I. When something is attributed by accident to causes which belong to them only per se. To this belong perplexity and abuse. Heresies have arisen from the reading of Scripture. Therefore laymen should not read it.

units.la: II. Quoties unius Effectus plures sunt causæ sive subordinatæ, sive pares, si una omissa, ponantur reliquæ, effectus non sequitur. V.G. Johanni & Petro Christianis pauper eleemosynam & stipem petens se se ad portam templi obtulit. E. ei stipem dederunt. Est fallacia ὡς τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον, quia non habebant unde darent.
units.tr: II. Whenever there are several causes of one effect, whether subordinate or coordinate, and if one is omitted and the rest are posited, the effect does not follow. For example: A poor man, asking alms, presented himself at the gate of the temple to John and Peter, who were Christians. Therefore they gave him alms. This is the fallacy of what is not a cause as if it were a cause [ὡς τὸ μὴ αἴτιον ὡς αἴτιον], because they had nothing to give.

units.la: Atque hic cum primis magnus est campus fallaciarum testimonii, quæ hujus loci sunt, & in Pontificia Theologia ubique obviæ.
units.tr: And here above all there is a large field of fallacies of testimony, which belong to this place and are found everywhere in Papist theology.

units.la: A. Cùm Scripturæ sensum affingunt, qui nusquam in illa extat. His fallaciis Evangelium suum referšit Xavier Jesuita.
units.tr: A. When they ascribe to Scripture a sense which is nowhere found in it. With these fallacies the Jesuit Xavier pressed his gospel.

units.la: B. Cùm libri Apocryphi citantur pro Canonicis. Ita Purgatorium, sanctorum invocationem, liberum arbitrium iidem stabiliunt.
units.tr: B. When the apocryphal books are cited as canonical. In this way the same men establish Purgatory, the invocation of saints, and free will.

units.la: C. Cùm Scripturæ sententias ignorantiâ Linguæ non intellectas male applicant, & defendendis omnibus inservire cogunt. His flosculis commentaria eorum scatent: Specimina dedimus alibi.
units.tr: C. When they wrongly apply sayings of Scripture which they have not understood because of ignorance of the languages, and compel them to serve in defending everything. Their commentaries teem with such flowers. We have given specimens elsewhere.

units.la: D. Quum mala consuetudine, authoritate Patrum, & exemplis, sine Scripturæ præcepto, pugnant. Quibus in Papatu mucronibus nihil est solennius.
units.tr: D. When they contend against Scripture by means of evil custom, the authority of the Fathers, and examples, without any command of Scripture. Among the weapons of Papacy nothing is more common than these.

units.la: E. Cùm miraculorum pompa opponitur expressæ S. Sc. literæ. Qua de re prolixè in Hist. nostra Ecclesiastica.
units.tr: E. When the pomp of miracles is set against the plain letter of Holy Scripture. On this matter at length in our Ecclesiastical History.

units.la: G. Fallacia à pluribus Interrogationibus est, cùm plures quæstiones confunduntur in unam. Unde Græci πολυζήτησιν vocant.
units.tr: G. The fallacy of many questions, which occurs when several questions are confused into one. Hence the Greeks call it polyzētēsin [πολυζήτησιν] (many-questioning).

units.la: Tripliciter hæc committitur fallacia I. cùm de uno subjecto plura interrogantur Prædicata, ut: Anne bona opera necessaria sunt & justificant? II. Cùm de pluribus subjectis quæritur unum prædicatum, ut: Sunt ne Deus & Mundus æterni? III. Cùm de pluribus subjectis quæruntur plura Prædicata; ut: Fuerunt ne Bullingerus & Bellarminus Theologi & Reformati? Referunt huc nonnulli ἐπηροζήτησιν, quæ & ἐπηροφνὲς & μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος dicitur, cùm à propositâ quæstione ad alienam deflectitur: quæ tamen aliud nihil est quàm Ignoratio Elenchi,
units.tr: This fallacy is committed in three ways. I. When several predicates are asked about one subject, as in: Are good works necessary and do they justify? II. When one predicate is asked about several subjects, as in: Are God and the World eternal? III. When several predicates are asked about several subjects, as in: Were Bullinger and Bellarmine theologians and Reformed? Some refer here the epērotēsin [ἐπηροζήτησιν], which is also called epērophnes [ἐπηροφνὲς] and metabasis eis allo genos [μετάβασις εἰς ἄλλο γένος], when one turns aside from the question proposed to an alien one. Yet this is nothing other than Ignorance of the Refutation (ignoratio elenchi).

units.la: XIII. Observandum autem, hac vulgo serie Fallacias Materiæ proponi, quæ ad unam tamen legem generalem referri possunt, quæ ita se habet: Omnis syllogismus qui vel pluribus vel paucioribus constat terminis, quàm tribus, Sophisticus est.
units.tr: XIII. It should be noted that these fallacies of matter are commonly set out in this order, although they can all be referred to one general rule, which is as follows: Every syllogism which has either more or fewer terms than three is sophistical.

units.la: Tradunt Logici, præter alios Canones Syllogisticos generales, hunc etiam: In Syllogismo tantùm sint tres termini, nec plures nec pauciores; qui quidem Canon Lydius est lapis omnium syllogismorum, ad quem impingitur, quoties aliqua occurrit ἀσυλλογιστία, quæ vel ex pluribus oritur terminis, ut cùm Fallacia committitur a. Homonymia, b. Amphiboliæ. e. Compositionis. f. Divisionis. g. Figuræ dictionis. h. Accentus. i. Accidentis. k. à dicto secundùm quid. l. Ignorationis Elenchi: vel ex paucioribus, duobus nempe. Sic fallunt, qui peccant petitione principii, fallacia consequentiæ, & fallacia à non causa ut causa, quæ ipsæ species à petitione principii non longè absunt. Unde etiam fit, ut in responsionibus & fallaciarum solutionibus non eadem ab omnibus observetur ratio. Quod aliis est petitio principii, à quibusdam refertur ad fallaciam à non causa ut causa, & sic in cæteris. Qua de re utilis illa Danæi admonitio: Unum & eundem syllogismum ex variis & diversis Elenchis solvi posse. Vide p.149.
units.tr: The logicians teach, besides other general canons of syllogism, this one also: In a syllogism there must be only three terms, neither more nor fewer. This canon is indeed the touchstone (Lydian stone) of all syllogisms, against which any instance of invalid syllogism is tested, whenever it arises either from more terms, as when the fallacy is committed by a. Homonymy, b. Amphiboly, c. Composition, d. Division, e. Figure of speech, f. Accent, g. Accident, h. What is said with qualification (a dicto secundum quid), i. Ignorance of the Refutation; or from fewer, namely two terms. Thus those deceive who commit begging the question (petitio principii), the fallacy of the consequence, and the fallacy of treating a non-cause as a cause, species which are themselves not far removed from begging the question. Hence it also happens that in answering and solving fallacies the same method is not observed by all. What to some is begging the question, others refer to the fallacy of treating a non-cause as a cause, and so on for the rest. On this matter is that useful admonition of Danaeus: One and the same syllogism can be solved from various and different refutations. See p. 149.

units.la: XIV. Est hæc fallaciarum enumeratio: Sequitur solutio, respiciens vel Formam, vel Materiam.
units.tr: XIV. This is the enumeration of fallacies. There follows the solution, which concerns either the Form or the Matter.

units.la: XV. Solutio Formæ est rejectio Syllogismi, indicato Canone syllogistico, in quem ejus forma seu Dispositio peccet.
units.tr: XV. The solution of Form is the rejection of a syllogism, by indicating the syllogistic canon which its form or arrangement violates.

units.la: XVI. Solutio Materiæ est, qua vitium in Syllogismi materia commissum ostenditur.
units.tr: XVI. The solution of Matter is that by which a fault committed in the matter of the syllogism is shown.

units.la: XVII. Estque vel dictionis, vel Rei.
units.tr: XVII. And this is either of the word or of the thing.

units.la: XVIII. Solutio Dictionis est, qua ambigua distinguimus, obscura explicamus, Phrases & sententias dubias dextrè interpretamur.
units.tr: XVIII. The solution of the word is that by which we distinguish ambiguous terms, explain obscure ones, and rightly interpret doubtful phrases and sentences.

units.la: Habet hæc solutio locum in fallaciis homonymiæ, Amphiboliæ & figuræ Dictionis.
units.tr: This solution has its place in the fallacies of homonymy, amphiboly and the figure of speech.

units.la: XIX. Solutio rei quinq; potissimum perficitur modis. 1. Informatione Conclusionis. Quę usurpanda, cùm committitur fallacia vel ignorationis Elenchi, vel plurium Interrogationum.
units.tr: XIX. The solution of the thing is effected chiefly in five ways. 1. By the information of the conclusion. This is to be used when the fallacy of either ignorance of the refutation or of several questions is committed.

units.la: 2. Indicatione petiti principii: usitat a, cùm idem per idem probatur, aut controversum per æquè aut magis controversum.
units.tr: 2. By pointing out begging the question: this is customary when the same thing is proved by the same, or the disputed by something equally or more disputed.

units.la: 3. Monstratione vitiosæ consequentiæ, cùm ostenditur infirmitas nexus seu consequentiæ in Majori.
units.tr: 3. By demonstrating a faulty consequence, when the weakness of the connection or consequence in the major premise is shown.

units.la: 4. Limitatione, quæ locum habet in fallaciis à dicto secundùm quid, & Accidentis.
units.tr: 4. By limitation, which has its place in the fallacies of what is said with qualification and of accident.

units.la: 5. Inficiatione: quæ est vel propositionis totius, vel universalitatis. Illå, vel Major, vel Minor simpliciter negatur: Hac inficiamur Propositione eam, quę pro universali ponitur, revera universalem esse: Quę tamen inficiatio non succedit, nisi per Instantiam exempli contrarii infringere possimus universalitatem.
units.tr: 5. By denial, which is either of the whole proposition or of its universality. Either the major or the minor is simply denied. By the latter we deny that the proposition which is put forward as universal is really universal. This denial, however, does not succeed unless we can break the universality by an instance of a contrary example.

units.la: F I N I S.
units.tr: THE END.
